name: Crater Lake National Park
blurb: Whitebark pine, nutcrackers and bears around a deep snow-fed caldera lake.

tip.title: Remove the nutcrackers
tip.text: Clark's nutcracker plants whitebark pine by forgetting cached seeds. Set Clark's nutcracker to -100% and watch whitebark pine, then the squirrels and bears that eat its seeds.

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Crater Lake, Crater Lake National Park, Pinus albicaulis). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.name: Fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen needles, dead wood and carcasses on the forest floor and in the lake, returning nutrients to the soil.
A tall pink wildflower of open and disturbed ground that deer and pikas eat.

nodes.name: Lake plankton
nodes.desc: Tiny floating algae in the lake that capture sunlight and start the lake food chain.
The most recorded large herbivore here. It browses shrubs and wildflowers such as fireweed, and is prey for bears.
Stores conifer cones in middens; bears raid these for whitebark pine seeds.
The most recorded bird here. It caches whitebark pine seeds and forgets enough of them to plant new trees.
A small seed and insect eater that is prey for martens, hawks, snakes and many others.

nodes.name: Pacific marten
nodes.desc: A forest predator that favours deep-snow country and hunts rodents and birds.
An omnivore that scavenges carrion and hunts small prey around the park.
A summer scavenger that feeds mostly on carrion such as dead deer.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats whitebark pine seeds raided from squirrel middens, as well as deer and carrion.
A soaring raptor that hunts marmots, pikas, mice and birds over open slopes and meadows.

story: Crater Lake in Oregon fills a caldera left when Mount Mazama collapsed about 7,700 years ago. At 1,949 feet it is the deepest lake in the United States. No rivers flow in or out, and rain and snow replace its water about every 150 years. It is known for its deep blue color.
matters: Its water is very clear because nothing flows in. It is the deepest lake in the Western Hemisphere by average depth.
